points: India delivered official remarks on the Political Declaration for Pandemic Prevention, Preparedness, and Response at the UN High-Level Meeting in New York.
The WHO Pandemic Agreement aims to ensure equitable access to countermeasures, stronger disease surveillance, and technology transfer globally.
The core debate pits High-Income Countries resisting mandatory tech transfers against Low- and Middle-Income Countries demanding guaranteed financing and distribution.
The Pathogen Access and Benefit-Sharing system remains the critical outstanding annex holding up final ratification of the agreement.
India holds a dual identity as the pharmacy of the world while remaining dependent on foreign Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients and advanced patents.
India champions equitable real-time access to countermeasures and strict respect for member-state sovereignty in implementing health policies.

sum.text:
Context: At the United Nations High-Level Meeting (UN HLM) in New York, India delivered official remarks on the Political Declaration for Pandemic Prevention, Preparedness, and Response (PPPR), reinforcing the WHO-led Pandemic Agreement (PA).
The WHO Pandemic Agreement, adopted by the World Health Assembly in May 2025, is an international framework to strengthen global pandemic prevention, preparedness and response (PPPR). It aims to ensure equitable access to vaccines, diagnostics and treatments, alongside stronger disease surveillance, technology transfer and resilient health systems.
Institutional Mandate: Negotiated under the auspices of the World Health Organization (WHO) to establish a legally binding international architecture to prevent a repeat of the inequities and supply bottlenecks witnessed during the COVID-19 pandemic.
The Adoption Benchmark: Formally adopted by 124 member states in 2025 (with zero negative votes and 11 abstentions), creating a global framework across surveillance, supply-chain resilience, and multilateral response.
The Pathogen Access and Benefit-Sharing (PABS) System: The critical outstanding annex holding up final ratification; it mandates that countries sharing pathogen genetic data must receive guaranteed, affordable shares of the resulting countermeasures (vaccines, diagnostics, therapeutics).
The Global Fault Line: Pits High-Income Countries (HICs resisting mandatory tech transfers and IP waivers) against Low- and Middle-Income Countries (LMICs demanding guaranteed financing and equitable distribution before committing to intrusive surveillance).
Dual Identity as Pharmacy of the World & IP Recipient: India manufactures a dominant share of global vaccine volume, yet the underlying patents for novel mRNA and advanced therapeutic platforms remain concentrated in Western pharmaceutical firms.
Upstream Supply Chain Vulnerabilities: Domestic formulation capabilities remain exposed to geopolitical shocks due to heavy import dependency on foreign Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients (APIs) and advanced manufacturing equipment.
Global Public Goods as Diplomatic Leverage: India’s continental-scale deployments—such as open-source digital health platforms and national laboratory grids—position it to export digital public infrastructure (DPI) to the Global South.
National Sovereignty Safeguards: Ensures global surveillance mandates under the One Health framework do not impose unfunded regulatory liabilities on domestic farming,…

texts.x: UPSC Syllabus: Gs Paper 3- Effects of liberalisation on the economy, changes in industrial policy and their effects on industrial growth. Introduction Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) supports India’s growth by bringing capital, technology, jobs and links to global markets. Gross inward FDI reached $94.8 billion in FY26, and India ranked 11th among global destinations. Yet…
Turning investment commitments into projects requires tackling State-level administrative bottlenecks

points: India recorded a gross inward FDI of $94.8 billion in FY26, ranking 11th globally according to UNCTAD.
Investment pledges face slow conversion into physical projects due to domestic friction between the Centre, States, and agencies.
International project finance remains a quarter below its 2021 peak, and India follows this global downward trend.
Greenfield data centre investments reached $7 billion in the first three quarters of 2025, lagging behind several nations.
Dolphin-like coordination challenges persist as DPIIT coordinates approvals without final decision-making power, making the 12-week deadline patchy.
Labour codes merging 29 laws face implementation delays because states must notify their own rules since labour is on the Concurrent List.
Quality Control Orders increased significantly to nearly 790 before some were withdrawn, posing compliance burdens on imported components.
Future free trade agreements with Canada, Brussels, and ongoing bilateral treaties need independent investor dispute resolution mechanisms.
sum.text:
India’s gross inward foreign direct investment (FDI) reached a record $94.8 billion in FY26, and the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) World Investment Report 2026 ranks India 11th among top FDI destinations. Yet pledges still convert slowly into built projects, because the remaining hurdles lie inside India, between the Centre and States and among its agencies.
Pledge versus project: A pledge becomes a working factory only after land, approvals, power, taxes and dispute settlement fall into place.
Global backdrop: International project finance (money raised for individual projects) is about a quarter below its 2021 peak, and India follows the trend.
Greenfield lag: India drew about $7 billion in greenfield data centre investment (new facilities built from scratch) in the first three quarters of 2025 , among the top ten but behind Thailand, Spain, South Korea, the United States and France.
Internal negotiations: The hurdles left are domestic: the Centre must agree with States, the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) with line Ministries, and central rules with State notifications.
The takeaway: Fixing these gaps helps Indian firms as much as foreign investors, so coordination is now the main reform task.
Approvals: DPIIT coordinates but does not decide, so a 12 week deadline set in May 2026 is met unevenly. Eg. Tata Electronics’ Dholera semiconductor facility shows coordination can work.
Courts: The Commercial Courts Act, 2015 and Mediation Act, 2023 sped up commercial disputes, and arbitration is now the corporate default. Smaller firms still rely on courts.
Labour codes: Parliament merged 29 labour laws into four codes, with Central Rules notified in May 2026 . Labour is a Concurrent List subject (both Centre and States legislate), so each State must notify rules. Gujarat moved first.
Tax certainty: The Taxation Laws (Amendment) Act, 2021 ended disputes over taxing past deals by withdrawing demands on Vodafone and Cairn Energy. A relaunched Vivad se Vishwas scheme cut the direct tax litigation backlog.
Quality Control Orders: These make Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) certification compulsory, like an ISI mark. Their number grew from under 70 to nearly 790 , the Gauba Committee found, before orders on PVC, aluminium and zinc were withdrawn.
Coming pacts: After the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi, December visits to Canada and Brussels are expected to see free trade agreements signed.

explain.headline: Adequate Response: On the RBI Rate Hike and Inflation Control
static: India operates under a Flexible Inflation Targeting (FIT) framework enshrined in the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934.
The monetary policy framework agreement between the Government of India and the RBI was signed in 2015 to adopt the FIT framework.
Section 45ZB of the amended RBI Act, 1934 provides for an empowered six-member Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) constituted by the Central Government in 2016.
The Government of India, in consultation with the RBI, sets the numerical inflation target at 4% with a tolerance band of plus or minus 2 percentage points.
The government and the RBI are required to review the FIT framework every five years, with the first review conducted in March 2021.

explain.background: India follows a Flexible Inflation Targeting framework managed by a six-member Monetary Policy Committee under the RBI Act, 1934.
significance: Signals the central bank's firm commitment to price stability and anchoring inflation expectations.
Addresses external vulnerabilities like capital outflows and currency depreciation caused by elevated US interest rates.
Poses challenges for borrowers through higher EMIs while offering marginal relief to savers through increased deposit rates.

UPSC Syllabus: GS-3-Indian Economy Context: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has raised the policy repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.50%, marking its…
The RBI policy review will need Central assistance to effectively fight inflation

points: The Reserve Bank of India raised the policy repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.50% and shifted its stance from neutral to calibrated tightening.
This is the first rate hike since February 2023, triggered by retail inflation remaining above the 4% medium-term target for three consecutive months.
The core issue is balancing inflation control through higher borrowing costs against maintaining sustainable economic growth amidst domestic and global uncertainties.
Retail inflation reached 4.82% in August, driven by rising food prices, weather disruptions, and drought concerns affecting agricultural output.
Global pressures include a crude oil price surge past $100 per barrel, geopolitical tensions in West Asia, and the ongoing Russia-Ukraine war.
External financial pressures stem from elevated US interest rates, higher US yields, and foreign investment outflows triggering currency pressures.
Domestic agricultural risks involve potential El Niño conditions extending into 2027 and reservoir levels dropping about 20% below the previous year.
The RBI revised its FY27 GDP growth projection upwards from 6.7% to 7.1% despite the tighter monetary policy stance.
The policy aims to contain inflation, anchor inflation expectations, manage external pressures, and prevent price increases from becoming entrenched.
sum.text:
Context: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has raised the policy repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.50%, marking its first rate hike since February 2023. The Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) has also shifted its policy stance from ‘neutral’ to ‘calibrated tightening’, indicating the possibility of further interest rate hikes depending on evolving economic conditions.
Repo rate is the rate at which the RBI lends money to commercial banks for a short period by repurchasing government securities from them.

points: India's urban centres face rising demands for infrastructure and public services due to rapid urbanisation and ageing infrastructure.
Property tax is the most important own-source revenue of municipal bodies, yet India's cumulative property tax is only 0.15-0.2 percent of GDP.
Property taxation involves three stages: enumeration, valuation and assessment, and billing and collection, with weaknesses at each stage.
Incomplete property enumeration, outdated records, and manual record-keeping reduce the accuracy of the tax base and limit municipal revenues.
Most municipalities use an area-based valuation using a base rate per square foot per month rather than linking tax to current market values.
Municipal base rates are revised infrequently compared with circle rates, leading to weak tax buoyancy and limited responsiveness of revenues.
Excessive exemptions for government properties and religious institutions further narrow the tax base and reduce municipal revenue collections.
Shortages of municipal staff, irregular municipal elections, and poor financial reporting severely limit effective property tax assessment and collection.
Structural reforms require strengthening human resources, combining technology with physical verification, rationalising exemptions, and ensuring timely municipal elections.

The Nifty Auto index declined more than 1% in the session, with major constituents including Maruti Suzuki, Tata Motors PV, M&M and Hyundai falling over 1% each. The Nifty Bank index slipped nearly 1%, down 0.70%. The Nifty Metal index also dropped more than 1%, with Tata Steel, Hindalco, Nalco and Vedanta among the major stocks falling up to 3% following the RBI's decision. The PSU Bank index and Nifty FMCG index also declined by up to 1%. What did RBI governor say? The RBI Governor said the re-escalation of the West Asia conflict has weighed on global economic sentiment, while the inflation outlook is less benign than it was last year. The Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) said recalibrating the policy rate is imperative, with four members voting in favour of a calibrated tightening stance. The MPC also indicated that rate cuts are off the table in the near term. The MPC noted that strong GDP growth and high credit growth pose risks of demand-side pressure on CPI inflation, although there is limited evidence of such pressure so far. It also observed some signs of generalised inflation and said it is difficult to distinguish supply-side inflation from the second-order effects of price shocks. The committee added that the second-round impact of supply shocks needs to be taken into account. RBI rate hike market impact The Indian stock market slipped into the red on Wednesday after a two-day relief rally, with Sensex and Nifty dropping up to 0.7% after RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra announced the central bank’s first rate hike in four years and changed stance to ‘calibrated tightening’. Sensex dropped more than 540 points to 72,520 while Nifty 50 lost 176 points to fall below 22,580 on Wednesday morning after Sanjay Malhotra’s announcement, dismissing near-term rate cuts. Broader markets were mixed, with Nifty Midcap 100 in the red and Nifty Smallcap 100 in the green. The rate hike comes as domestic inflation remains above the RBI's 4% target, while elevated crude oil prices add another external risk. points: Munna, a male tiger in Kanha Tiger Reserve, lived to age 19 and attracted millions of visitors due to forehead stripes resembling the word CAT.
Central Indian folklore and modern parks show a long history of naming iconic tigers like Lungra, Kankati, and Machli based on unique features.
Research in Frontiers in Ecology and Environment labels such animals with unique traits as flagship individuals, serving as ambassadors for their species.
In Achanakmar Tiger Reserve, a tigress named Jhumri migrated from Bandhavgarh and helped double the local tiger population.
An Assam elephant known as Ramu shifted from being a maligned crop-raider to an object of local affection before dying of electrocution.
Flagship individuals create vital emotional connections between humans and wildlife, driving legal actions, funding, and conservation policies.

sum.text:
M unna, a male tiger, died at the ripe old age of 19. He spent 17 years in the wilds of Kanha Tiger Reserve, where he held his territory and sired many cubs . He attracted attention as a male in his prime in the late 2000s, bearing perhaps the most iconic of marks borne by any tiger — stripes that resembled the word ‘ CAT ’on his forehead. No one can calculate how much revenue the reserve generated from tourists who flocked for a glimpse of Munna alone. A quick internet search, however, shows over three million hits for his photographs, and he is immortalised in many books. Munna’s story continued after his death. The cubs he sired – Neelam, Chhota Munna, Umarpani male, among the many – became a fixation for visitors. This is not unheard of; people have tracked and mapped tigers’ lineages across several generations. A century ago, the peoples of Central India identified tigers by their features – Lungra, the limping tiger, Tajia bagh, the small-eared tiger, Banda bagh, the tailless tiger, and Dhor bagh, the cattle-eating tiger, were some common names popularised in folklore. Fast forward to today, the essence remains the same – Kankati and Machli, both iconic tigers of Ranthambore, were named after their features. Show Full Article

points: The Monetary Policy Committee of the Reserve Bank of India increased the policy repo rate by 25 basis points.
The decision aligns with expectations and acknowledges the tension between resilient domestic momentum and a turbulent external environment.
India's GDP growth forecast for the fiscal year has been revised upwards from 6.7% to 7.1%.
The inflation forecast has been moved up from 5% to 5.2% alongside an upward revision in expected crude oil prices.
The RBI mandate aims to ensure that inflation does not become widespread amid a tight-for-long monetary pivot in advanced economies.
The policy stance changed to calibrated tightening, signaling that near-term rate cuts are off the table with future actions limited to hikes or pauses.
The MPC noted that rate hikes help tackle supply-side constraints, which are identified as the primary source of current inflation.
Government absorption of fuel and fertilizer costs has cushioned inflation at the expense of fiscal numbers, creating potential headwinds during future consolidation.
sum.text:
That the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) would increase the policy rate was a given. It has done so by 25 basis points, in keeping with expectations. What was watched more keenly was MPC’s prognosis of the larger economic situation.
On that front, it has not held back from underlining the inherent tension in the Indian economy: resilient domestic momentum against a multi-faceted turbulent external economic environment. India’s growth forecast for the fiscal year has been revised upwards from 6.7% to 7.1%. The biannual Monetary Policy Review says that unless there is a major disruption, GDP growth will be 7% in 2027-28 .
The inflation forecast has been moved up from 5% to 5.2%. Expected crude oil prices have also been revised upwards. RBI also believes that elevated bond yields and AI-driven equity asset valuations in advanced markets are not going away anytime soon.
RBI’s mandate, given the situation, was to ensure that inflation does not become — and more importantly, is not seen as becoming — widespread. India’s monetary policy cannot be seen as oblivious to what clearly looks like a tight-for-long monetary pivot in advanced economies. The change in policy stance to calibrated tightening — the Governor has clearly said this means rate cuts are off the table in the near term and policy action ahead can only be a rate hike or a pause — is a good way to approach the problem.
MPC has clearly conveyed its stance that it will not sit back and let inflation escalate but also decided against being seen as dogmatically pursuing inflation by raising rates. That the MPC resolution talks about how rate hikes tackle supply side constraints — the source of most of the current inflation — is yet another example of this approach. All said, MPC’s latest decision is anything but drastic when seen in comparison to the prevailing external economic situation, especially in commodity and capital markets.
This also raises an interesting question. India’s inflation story would have been much worse had the government decided to pass on the full cost of increased fuel or fertilizer prices to consumers. The pain has been offset by passing a large cost to the fiscal numbers.
We will know more about this closer to the budget. A consolidation next year may also create headwinds for growth.

sum.text:
The timing of the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement (MJDA) signed between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey in August was hard to ignore. It came into existence when the war in West Asia involving Iran raised apparent scepticism towards the reliability of American security assurances in the Gulf region. The language of the agreement seemed deliberately broad-based, with the most striking clause stating that an armed attack against one member would be regarded as an attack on all. The stated purpose was to strengthen collective deterrence.
The act, established on a political commitment and defence cooperation framework, still lacks a robust institutional foundation and has no operational experience. The misaligned threat perceptions of Islamabad, Riyadh, and Ankara lend more credence to the pact's ambiguity.
Following the sustained Yemeni Houthi-led attacks on Saudi Arabia's cities, ports, and energy facilities, on October 5, the defence and foreign ministers of MJDA member states met in Riyadh for an emergency session of the Strategic Political and Defence Committee (SPDC) under the pact. The states agreed to move to a practical implementation of the defence commitments to ensure rapid deployment of agreed forces and capabilities in the Kingdom, "in accordance with the national legislation of the parties". The Foreign Office described this as the first invocation of the bloc since its signing.
The agreement was signed in August. Since then, the three governments have been establishing institutions, appointing mechanisms, holding meetings between defence officials and military chiefs, discussing intelligence cooperation, and reportedly working towards integration of capabilities. The September meeting of military chiefs and the October meeting of the SPDC show that the institutional groundwork is being done. In that context, to view the pact as merely symbolic or to label it an ‘Islamic NATO' understates or overstates its current reality. Instead, the recent announcement indicates the alliance is rapidly acquiring operational meaning. The timelines are trying to keep up with the hostilities around it.
For Pakistan, the challenge will remain in how delicately it can honour the pact - which could include protecting the Kingdom but not directly targeting Yemen. points: External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar raised questions on how India can de-risk, diversify, and extract value from existing partnerships amidst changing US-China ties.
The author argues that moving from resilience to action requires connecting domestic strength with external engagement and constantly reassessing foreign policy assumptions.
The core issue is that interdependence can become an instrument of coercion, and traditional labels like allies and adversaries do not guarantee diplomatic outcomes.
Jaishankar highlighted a world where the US and China are competitors but are also engaged in a certain conversation, creating uncertainty for other nations.
Strategic autonomy requires building domestic economic strength, technological competence, and capable institutions so that the costs of independent choices are not prohibitive.
Diversification must create usable alternatives and reduce vulnerabilities rather than just accumulating a large number of diplomatic partnerships.
India must identify critical dependencies that could constrain national interests and bear short-term costs to preserve future freedom of action.
Cooperation with the Global South can help countries withstand external pressure and exercise greater agency in an eroding rules-based international order.
sum.text:
R esilience has become a familiar word in international affairs. But its strategic meaning rests on a harder question: when external circumstances change, can a country sustain the pursuit of its interests on its own terms? For India, moving from the language of resilience to resilience in action means matching national ambition with the capacity to carry it forward. This calls for a grand strategy that connects domestic strength with external engagement and continually reassesses the assumptions guiding India’s choices abroad. The challenge is sharper in an international order where power remains concentrated, interdependence can become an instrument of coercion, and commitments are open to renewed bargaining. Alliances, partnerships and adversaries are still consequential categories, but these labels alone cannot tell India what a relationship will deliver. A partner may enhance its security while narrowing its economic choices. A competitor may remain important to its development. An accommodation between major powers may reshape the choices of countries with no seat at the negotiating table. India’s strategy must continually assess what these overlapping realities mean for its interests and room for manoeuvre. A circular economy is an economic model that aims to minimise waste and maximise the reuse, repair, refurbishment and recycling of products and materials. It seeks to keep resources in use for as long as possible while reducing pressure on natural resources and the environment.
Design out waste and pollution: Products should be designed to minimise waste, pollution and the use of hazardous materials throughout their lifecycle.
Keep products and materials in use: Products should remain useful for as long as possible through reuse, repair, refurbishment, remanufacturing and recycling.
Regenerate natural systems: Economic activities should restore rather than continuously degrade natural resources and ecosystems.
Resource efficiency: Maximum economic value should be obtained from minimum quantities of raw materials, energy and water.
Extended product life: Products should be durable, repairable and upgradeable to reduce premature disposal.
Waste as a resource: Waste from one process should become an input for another wherever technically and economically feasible.
Renewable and sustainable inputs: Greater reliance should be placed on renewable energy and sustainably sourced materials to reduce dependence on finite resources.
Conserves natural resources : The circular economy promotes the reuse, repair, refurbishment and recycling of products and materials, thereby reducing the need for continuous extraction of virgin resources. A 25-basis-point repo rate hike may look small, but it can have a meaningful impact on borrowing costs, household budgets and financial markets. With the 25-bps increase, the repo rate stands at 5.50%, marking the first rate hike since February 2023.
The RBI’s repo rate is the rate at which commercial banks borrow funds from the central bank. When the RBI raises it, borrowing becomes more expensive for banks, which can eventually translate into higher lending rates for consumers and businesses.
Adhil Shetty, CEO, BankBazaar, said: “The RBI has raised the repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.50%, the first increase since February 2023. It has also moved to a stance of calibrated tightening, signalling that future moves will depend on how inflation and economic conditions evolve. For borrowers, the impact is likely to be gradual. The latest increase is only a fraction of the 125 basis points of cuts delivered earlier, so much of the earlier EMI relief remains in place. Savers could benefit as banks gradually reprice deposits, while borrowers should check how quickly their lender passes on the rate change.”
Kumar Binit, CEO, airpay money, said: “A 25-basis-point hike to 5.50%, coming just ahead of Diwali, could put some additional pressure on household budgets. Floating-rate borrowers may see higher EMIs or longer loan tenures, while depositors could benefit as banks gradually reprice fixed deposits. For households receiving festive bonuses or seasonal income, higher deposit rates could make short- to medium-term fixed-income options more attractive.”
Upasna Bhardwaj, Chief Economist, Kotak Mahindra Bank, said: “The MPC delivered a 25-basis-point rate hike in line with expectations, but the shift towards calibrated tightening is the more important signal for markets. We continue to see the possibility of further rate hikes, with the extent depending on the inflation trajectory and global risks.”

The 57th Goods and Services Tax (GST) Council meeting in New Delhi on Oct 8 is expected to discuss major reforms aimed at simplifying compliance, accelerating refunds and reducing regulatory burdens on businesses. According to media reports, the agenda includes easier registration, streamlined Input Tax Credit (ITC) procedures, decriminalisation of offences and changes to the definition of service exports. The proposals are expected to benefit businesses across agriculture, manufacturing, exports and micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs).
GST Rules Set For Major Overhaul, Know- What Could Get Cheaper & Easier For Businesses? GST Council may review arrest powers and export rulesOne significant proposal involves removing the standalone arrest provisions under Section 69 of the Central Goods and Services Tax (CGST) Act, Moneycontrol reported. Currently, the GST commissioner can authorise arrests when there are reasons to believe that specified offences, including fraudulent invoicing, wrongful ITC claims and tax evasion, have occurred.
The council is expected to consider withdrawing these powers from tax authorities during investigations. Another proposal seeks to broaden the definition of service exports. Under the proposed changes, Indian companies could retain export status when billing overseas clients through foreign branches.
Services performed in India for international customers could also qualify as exports. The move could benefit global capability centres (GCCs), which provide engineering, product development and testing services to multinational companies. Some such services currently attract 18% GST because of rules determining their place of supply.
Qualifying them as exports could remove this tax liability. Faster GST refunds and simplified registration proposed. The council is also expected to examine measures to accelerate GST refunds and improve business cash flow.

sum.text:
Scientists Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry on Wednesday for solving a long-standing puzzle involving asymmetric "mirror image" molecules, a breakthrough with major implications for pharmaceutical manufacturing.
Soai, 76, is Japanese, while Kagan, 95, is French. Their work built on the discoveries of 19th-century French chemist Louis Pasteur. Kagan is the third-oldest person to receive a Nobel Prize.
"This is the most exciting day in my life. I am very glad to share this prize with Professor Henri Kagan," Soai said by phone during the Nobel Prize press conference. He added that he had been out grocery shopping when he received the news.
Kagan's daughter, Veronique Le Deunff, said she was "very happy", adding that her father's "creativity and originality" had opened new avenues for research.
French President Emmanuel Macron congratulated the laureates on X, describing the award as an immense honour for France. "A recognition suited to a lifetime of research," he said.
Kagan's work had long been regarded as influential in the field. In 2001, the then-French research minister complained to the Nobel Foundation after Kagan was not awarded the prize that year. The Nobel instead went to two American scientists and one Japanese scientist for work in the same field.
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi also congratulated Soai during a phone call. "As a Japanese, I'm very proud of you," she told him.
Many molecules essential to life exist in two forms that are mirror images of one another, much like a person's left and right hands. Living organisms, however, almost exclusively use just one of these forms, a phenomenon known as "homochirality", derived from the Greek word for hand.
This year's Nobel recognised discoveries showing how chemical reactions can be controlled to favour one molecular mirror image over the other. The work has proved important for chemists developing reactions used in pharmaceutical manufacturing.
"The left-handed version of the drug can have one effect, and the right-handed version can have another effect, and then we need methods for selectively preparing them," said Peter Somfai, a member of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry.
"In developing such methods, the findings of this year's laureates are important. They provided powerful tools for that," he added.
The first major link in the chain came from Pasteur, who died several years before the Nobel Prizes were first awarded in 1901.

The Supreme Court on Thursday observed that regulations governing the appointment of the Director General of Police (DGP) in Jharkhand appeared to be in conflict with the principles laid down in the case of Prakash Singh v. .A Bench of Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V Mohana made the observation while hearing an application filed by the Central government challenging the Selection and Appointment of Director General and Inspector General of Police, Jharkhand (Head of Police Force) Regulations, 2025 and all DGP appointments made under it. In particular, the Central government flagged that the regulations permit the appointment of police officers with less than six months till retirement to be appointed as DGPs.
In March 2019, the top court passed an order as part of the Prakash Singh case (on police reforms) by which it clarified that only officers who have at least six months of service remaining prior to their retirement should be recommended to the post of DGP.The Centre flagged a violation of this principle in the appointment of DGPs in the State, including its incumbent DGP Tadasha Mishra, who was appointed to the post for a two year term a day before she was slated to retire from service. The Court today said that the appointment appears to conflict with the Prakash Singh ruling. "An officer has been made eligible to be considered for appointment as Director General of Police of the State even where the residual service before superannuation is less than six months.
Such a provision, prima facie, appears to be directly in conflict with the law laid down by this Court in Prakash Singh," the Court said..The Court proceeded to grant the Jharkhand government one week's time to either revisit its DGP appointment rule or defend it. "Our concern is not who is in power at the Centre or State. Our bounden duty is to ensure that the law declared by this Court is not diluted," said Justice Bagchi..The Court also sought a response from DGP Tadasha Mishra." A right has already been created in her favour.
If we set aside the rule, that may have consequences for her appointment. Otherwise, we can set aside the rule prospectively and say that the officer shall continue," explained CJI Kant. sum.text:
The Union Cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, on Friday approved the Pradhan Mantri Surya Sarovar Yojana (PM-SSY), a ₹5,070 crore scheme to accelerate the development of floating solar photovoltaic (FSPV) projects integrated with energy storage systems across the country.
In a post on X, PM Modi said, “The Cabinet’s approval of the Pradhan Mantri Surya Sarovar Yojana expands India’s clean-energy capacity through the innovative use of our reservoirs and inland water bodies. The Scheme will benefit every State and Union Territory and reduce CO₂ emissions.”
The scheme aims to develop 5,000 MW of floating solar capacity along with 10,000 MWh of co-located energy storage, providing a minimum storage duration of two hours. Projects will be sanctioned between FY 2026-27 and FY 2030-31, while financial assistance will continue to be disbursed until FY 2032-33.
The approval follows an assessment by the National Institute of Solar Energy (NISE), which estimated India’s floating solar potential at around 102.18 GWp across reservoirs and other suitable inland water bodies.
Under the scheme, the Centre will provide Central Financial Assistance (CFA) of ₹1 crore per MW for eligible floating solar projects after successful commissioning. In addition, project developers can receive up to ₹50 lakh per project for feasibility studies, including bathymetry and hydrography surveys, environmental assessments and other preparatory activities aimed at reducing project risks.
The government said the scheme will benefit all States and Union Territories while significantly expanding India’s floating solar capacity, which currently stands at around 700 MW. By utilising reservoirs and industrial ponds, the initiative is expected to reduce dependence on scarce land resources for renewable energy projects.
The integration of energy storage systems is expected to strengthen grid reliability by improving the availability and stability of renewable power.
The scheme is projected to reduce nearly 10 million tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions annually and generate around 16,000-17,000 full-time equivalent employment opportunities across the project value chain.
The initiative is also expected to boost domestic manufacturing of floating platforms, photovoltaic cells and modules, energy storage systems and other key components, supporting the government’s Aatmanirbhar Bharat initiative.

explain.headline: GST Council Meeting 2026: Arrest Powers Scrapped and Prosecution Threshold Raised
static: The Goods and Services Tax (GST) Council is a constitutional body established under Article 279A of the Constitution, introduced by the 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016.
The Council is chaired by the Union Finance Minister, with the Minister of State for Finance and state Finance or Taxation Ministers as members.
It is designed to make recommendations to the Union and State Governments on key GST issues, tax rates, exemptions, thresholds, and dispute resolution mechanisms.
Decisions in the GST Council require a weighted majority of not less than three-fourths of the votes cast, where the Centre has one-third weightage and all states combined have two-thirds weightage.

explain.background: The GST Council governs indirect tax policies and rates across India, functioning through a cooperative federalism framework between the Centre and States.
significance: Reduces the risk of criminalisation for routine business disputes by eliminating arrest powers and lifting prosecution limits.
Improves working capital management and ease of doing business through automated refunds and simplified e-commerce and transit rules.

The GST Council recently approved substantial reforms to simplify the indirect tax structure and improve compliance. These changes include raising prosecution thresholds and decriminalising several offences, signifying a major shift in GST law. Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman outlined plans for these reforms to take effect from April 1 next year. Experts believe these measures will enhance business operations and support economic growth.

On input tax credit claims, the 57th GST Council decided to set up a Committee of Officers to examine how to protect a genuine buyer who holds a proper invoice, has received the goods, and has paid his supplier in full.
The council proposed raising the prosecution threshold from ₹1 crore to ₹5 crore, meaning cases involving amounts below ₹5 crore would not lead to prosecution.

points: The GST Council approved sweeping enforcement and procedural reforms under GST 2.0 to ease compliance, making no changes to tax rates.
The Council removed the power of arrest under GST and raised the prosecution threshold from Rs 1 crore to Rs 5 crore.
The general penalty under GST was reduced from Rs 25,000 to Rs 10,000, addressing business concerns over the criminalisation of routine disputes.
Registration and refund timelines were streamlined, with 90% of refund claims to be sanctioned automatically within three working days of acknowledgement.
Transit inspection rules were eased, allowing vehicles to be stopped only on specific intelligence and solely by origin and destination states.
An optional compliance scheme was approved for small taxpayers with up to Rs 5 crore turnover supplying exclusively to consumers, allowing annual returns and quarterly tax payments.
ITC was extended to ordinary business spending like employee health insurance, telecommunication towers, pipelines, free samples, and stock written off after expiry.
Export benefits were expanded for Indian companies serving foreign clients via overseas branches and for work done in India on goods belonging to foreign clients.
sum.text:
The GST Council on Thursday approved a sweeping set of enforcement and procedural reforms aimed at easing compliance for businesses, with key decisions including the removal of arrest powers under GST, a five-fold increase in the prosecution threshold and a series of measures to simplify registration, returns, refunds and input tax credit.

New Delhi [India] October 8 (ANI): The Central Armed Police Forces (General Administration) Act, 2026 (9 of 2026), officially came into force on Thursday, establishing a statutory framework to regulate recruitment and service conditions for Group A General Duty officers and personnel across the CAPFs. The Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) issued the enforcement notification under sub-section (2) of Section 1 of the Act: "In exercise of the powers conferred by sub-section (2) of section 1 of the Central Armed Police Forces (General Administration) Act, 2026 (9 of 2026), the Central Government hereby appoints the 08th day of October, 2026, as the date on which the provisions of the said Act shall come into force."
The legislation previously received presidential assent from President Droupadi Murmu on April 9, after passing through the Rajya Sabha on April 1 and the Lok Sabha on April 2. Top command postings in Central Armed Police Forces (CAPFs) will now be governed by explicit statutory law, with the Act coming into effect from today. Under the new law, 50 per cent of Inspector General (IG) posts have been reserved for Indian Police Service (IPS) officers on deputation.
For the rank of Additional Director General (ADG), at least 67 per cent of posts will be reserved for IPS deputationists. At the apex level, the posts of Special Director General (SDG) and Director General (DG) will be 100 per cent reserved for IPS officers. Earlier, these postings were governed by executive orders. The Central Government highlighted that CAPFs operate under strict command structures with operational requirements distinct from other organisations due to their role in border security and internal law enforcement.
Minister of State for Home, Nityanand Rai, who replied to the discussion on the bill then, had said the legislation would bring administrative clarity and was not against the interests of the Central Armed Police Force (CAPF) officers and would ensure promotion and financial benefits for the cadre. sum.text:
Indian households expect inflation to reach 10 per cent over the next one year, up from 9.4 per cent in July, reflecting growing concerns over rising prices at a time when the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has begun raising interest rates to contain inflation. According to the RBI's September 2026 Inflation Expectations Survey of Households, the median inflation expectation for the next 12 months increased by 60 basis points to 10 per cent, while the three-month expectation rose by 70 basis points to 9.9 per cent from 9.2 per cent in July.
The RBI said, "Households’ median inflation expectations for the next three months and one year rose by 70 bps and 60 bps to 9.9 per cent and 10.0 per cent, respectively." The findings come as the RBI's Monetary Policy Committee raised the repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 per cent on October 7 amid inflation concerns.
Rising household inflation expectations are significant because they reflect growing concerns about future living costs and can influence consumer spending and wage expectations, making them an important indicator for monetary policy. The survey also showed that households' perception of current inflation increased to 8.4 per cent in September from 7.8 per cent in July.
"The current median inflation perception of households increased by 60 basis points (bps) to 8.4 per cent as compared to the previous round," RBI said. Concerns about future price increases also strengthened. As many as 88.9 per cent of respondents expected general prices to rise over the next year, while 67.4 per cent anticipated prices increasing at a faster pace than currently.
Over the next three months, 81.9 per cent expected prices to increase, compared with 80.7 per cent in July. Food prices remained a major concern, with 84.9 per cent expecting food prices to rise over the next three months. Of these surveyed households, 61.6 per cent of all respondents expected food prices to increase faster than at present.
The RBI noted that "The proportion of respondents anticipating a rise in general inflation has inched up for both the time horizons." The survey highlights persistent inflation concerns among households even as monetary policy has turned tighter. However, the 10 per cent figure represents households' median expectation and should not be interpreted as the RBI's official inflation forecast.
The survey was conducted between September 10 and 20 across 19 major cities, covering 5,987 respondents. (ANI)

sum.text:
New Delhi: More than 16 lakh small businesses that sell directly to consumers could soon be allowed to file just one GST return annually, after the GST Council on Thursday approved in principle a simplified compliance scheme for taxpayers with turnover of up to Rs 5 crore. Under the proposed framework, eligible businesses such as retail shops, salons and small eateries would pay GST every quarter but file a single return each year, reducing compliance requirements for a segment that accounts for less than 1 per cent of total GST liability. The proposal, cleared at the 57th GST Council meeting chaired by Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman, will be available as an optional scheme for taxpayers with annual turnover of up to Rs 5 crore. Under the proposed framework, eligible businesses would file a single GST return each year while paying taxes on a quarterly basis. Officials said the detailed operational framework and the legislative amendments required to implement the scheme will be placed before the Council at its next meeting. The reforms are slated to take effect from April 1, 2027. The proposed scheme is expected to benefit a large number of small businesses that deal exclusively with retail consumers, such as neighbourhood shops, salons, restaurants and small eateries. According to government estimates, out of 1.05 crore active GST taxpayers, around 16.85 lakh report supplies only to consumers. Of these, nearly 16.66 lakh taxpayers, or 99 per cent, have annual turnover below Rs 5 crore. Despite their large numbers, these businesses account for less than 1 per cent of the overall GST tax liability. Since their customers are individual consumers who do not claim input tax credit, the returns filed by such sellers have limited impact on the broader GST credit chain, making them suitable candidates for a simplified compliance regime. At present, GST taxpayers are generally required to file monthly returns. Businesses with turnover of up to Rs 5 crore have already been allowed to opt for quarterly return filing since 2021, although they continue to pay taxes every month. The new proposal seeks to simplify compliance further by reducing return filing to once a year while retaining quarterly tax payments.

New Delhi: The Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, in collaboration with the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports and the Ministry of Defence, on Thursday launched the JOSH (Joint Squad for Health) Teams at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi to strengthen community-led efforts towards eliminating tuberculosis (TB).
Addressing the gathering, Union Health Minister J.P. Nadda thanked the Sports Department and the Defence Ministry for supporting the initiative and said that 58,000 volunteers would work at the grassroots level. "I want to express my heartfelt thanks to the Sports Department and the Defence Ministry, who turned this vision into reality. Today, the Joint Squad for Health (JOSH) Team has been established, and our 58,000 volunteers will go from village to village to work. For this, I want to thank and congratulate you all," Nadda said.
"We don't want to limit this movement. The government, communities and citizens should come together. For a TB-free India, we should create awareness among people. It is not enough that we only create awareness and conduct screening. We also have to ensure diagnosis and treatment, increase community participation and come up with new and innovative ideas. We will have to complete this mission," he said.
Nadda also stressed the need to identify people who may be unaware that they have TB, including those who are asymptomatic. Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta said that a healthy population was essential for achieving the goal of a developed and prosperous India.
"As we are moving forward towards a prosperous India, it is not possible if we are not healthy. It is not possible to become developed if the people are not healthy," she said.
Gupta said the JOSH Teams would bring together young volunteers, NCC cadets, public representatives and government officials to work towards eliminating TB.
"When the JOSH Teams work together, and our young volunteers, NCC cadets, public representatives and officials go among the people and fight this battle against TB, we will be able to completely eradicate TB from the country," she said. "Health, youth and defence are our 'Trishakti'. The way they are working together, we are on a national mission," she added.

sum.text:
The government on Thursday rejected allegations that India’s regulatory framework for satellite communication services was discriminatory, asserting that all three global satellite communication companies were currently at broadly the same stage of the regulatory process.
The clarification came after Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk accused unnamed “oligarchs” of blocking Starlink’s entry into India to protect their “monopolistic chokehold” over the Indian market. In a post on X, Musk alleged that Starlink was being prevented from launching its satellite internet services in India and described the situation as “a crime against the people of India”. “Unfortunately, we are being blocked by certain oligarchs in order to maintain their monopolistic chokehold on the Indian people. You can guess who they are,” Musk said.
Responding to the allegations, the government said, "A post is being circulated in social media regarding the fairness of India’s regulatory framework for satellite communication services and suggesting that it is being applied in a discriminatory manner". The government said it has established a “fair and non-discriminatory” authorisation framework for all telecommunication services, including satellite communication services.
"Under this, telecom licences have been granted to three Global Mobile Personal Communication by Satellite services based on non-geosynchronous satellite orbit-based satellite communications, as part of its commitment to enable provision of satellite communication services in India," the government said in a statement.
The government said "each licensee is required to demonstrate compliance with security conditions" before proceeding further in the regulatory process. The security assessment is intended to ensure that satellite-based services meet various requirements related to the safety and security of users and their data. “Security assessment as part of this process is currently under way in respect of all the three licensees,” the government said. It added that once the security assessment is completed for a licensed entity, it can proceed to the next stage of seeking spectrum assignment. “At present, all the three entities are at broadly the same regulatory stage,” the government said, asserting that the suggestion that the regulatory framework or its application is unfair or discriminatory is “baseless and misconceived.”

sum.text:
Accra (Ghana), Oct 7 (PTI) Ghana's Cabinet has approved a decision to seek membership of BRICS and the country will now formally apply to join the grouping, the African nation’s Foreign Minister Sam Okudzeto Ablakwa said on Wednesday, with India's External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar saying New Delhi has been "very sympathetic and supportive" of Accra's aspirations.
Jaishankar arrived in Ghana on Tuesday on the first leg of his three-nation tour of African countries, which also includes Cote d'Ivoire and Ethiopia. Ghana's BRICS announcement came as Jaishankar held talks with its leadership during his visit.
Jaishankar and Ablakwa together addressed the media on Wednesday after their meeting.
Ablakwa said Ghana's decision was aimed at diversifying its international partnerships and giving the country more options in its development agenda, while stressing that it would not abandon its traditional partners such as the IMF and World Bank.
"We want to have options. We are not going to walk away from our traditional partners. We value that relationship, but we must have new friends," he said.
The foreign minister said Ghana also wanted to strengthen ties with historical partners such as India, Brazil and China, which already have significant trade and investment engagement with the West African country.
He said Ghana's trade with India had more than doubled, from around USD 3 billion in 2024, and that the country was seeking to take it to around USD 7 billion.
Ablakwa said BRICS membership would give Ghana greater options as it seeks to transform its economy, create jobs and industrialise, and advance what he described as an agenda of resource sovereignty.
He further said Ghana wanted to work with partners with shared interests and commitments and believed its BRICS aspirations aligned with President John Dramani Mahama's foreign policy priorities and his vision of a multipolar world.
Ghana will now take steps to formally apply for membership and seek the support of existing BRICS members, Ablakwa said, noting that admission would ultimately require the approval of the grouping.
Jaishankar, adding to Ablakwa's response, said BRICS brings together countries that value independence of thought and freedom of choice and that it was understandable that the grouping's message would resonate in different parts of the world.

Ships of Indian Coast Guard, Navy, helicopters and dornier aircrafts of Coast Guard, 130J of the Indian Air Force, vehicles of Customs and other agencies and stakeholders took part in the spectacular SAREX 26 maritime search and rescue operations with superior coordination and meticulous execution of the whole process.
In an exclusive interview with Akashvani News on board the ICGS Samudra Pratap, the DG of the Indian Coast Guard said the Coast Guard is ready to take the maritime search and rescue operations to a new height. He said the Indian Coast Guard took the foreign observers on board to plan the SAREX 26 event for the purpose of engaging the foreign partners in real-time search and rescue operations in the future. 32 observers from 30 friendly foreign countries today witnessed the SAREX 26 event.
In an exclusive interaction with Akashvani News, Blaise Taylor, Superintendent of the Australian Border Force, said on board ICGS Samudra Pratap that the Indian Coast Guard is showcasing a leading role in search and rescue operations. explain.headline: Supreme Court Allows Union of India's Appeals in Excise Incentive Withdrawal Case
static: Promissory estoppel is an equitable doctrine that prevents a party from going back on a promise if another party relied on it to their detriment.
In administrative law, the doctrine cannot be invoked to compel the government to act contrary to public interest or statutory provisions.
Article 248 of the Constitution and related legislative entries empower Parliament to make laws regarding taxes and excise duties.
Tax exemptions are conditional concessions granted by the state and can be curtailed, modified, or withdrawn when public interest demands.
The Supreme Court of India is the highest constitutional court and court of appeal under Article 136 of the Constitution.
explain.what: The Supreme Court allowed the Union of India's appeals in an excise incentive withdrawal case, ruling that the policy change was prospective and justified in the public interest.
explain.why_in_news: The Supreme Court delivered its verdict upholding the government's withdrawal of excise incentives.
explain.background: The case involves challenges to the government's withdrawal of excise tax exemptions, testing the boundaries of promissory estoppel against sovereign powers in public interest.
significance: Reinforces the primacy of public interest over individual claims based on promissory estoppel against the state.
Provides legal clarity for the government to adjust economic and tax policies dynamically.
Serves as an important legal precedent for taxation and administrative law disputes in India.
prelims: The Supreme Court allowed the appeals of the Union of India.
The impugned notification was held to be prospective.
Promissory estoppel was held not to bar the government policy change.
explain.mains: Examine the applicability of the doctrine of promissory estoppel against the government in matters of taxation and public policy with reference to recent judicial pronouncements.
